vignette: Maria is a 75-year-old Oceania woman who has lived through significant trauma during her time in a war zone. As an auditor, she was often required to travel between different locations for work, and it was during one such journey that the traumatic event unfolded. The day started like any other; Maria was on her way to a meeting at a remote location when a sudden attack occurred. She remembers the smell of sweat and body odour mingling with the acrid scent of smoke and gunfire. The images are etched in her mind, as clear as photographs, replaying over and over again. In the months following the event, Maria found that certain triggers evoked vivid memories. When she felt happy or relaxed, the joy would abruptly fade away as the images from that day resurfaced. Her workplace, with its sterile smell and precise order, became a constant reminder of the chaos she had experienced. The olfactory cues were particularly potent; even the faintest whiff of sweat or body odour transported her back to that moment. Maria has come to believe that others can see what happened to her just by looking at her. She feels exposed, as if there is an indelible mark on her that everyone else sees but cannot speak about. This belief exacerbates her sense of vulnerability and leads her to adopt several maladaptive strategies. She often ruminate over how the event could have been prevented and why it happened to her, which only reinforces the feeling that she will never be able to feel normal emotions again. Her life feels less worthwhile as these thoughts loop endlessly in her mind. Maria's fear of being seen has led her to rehearse conversations before any interaction, a strategy that provides temporary relief but ultimately serves as a reminder of the trauma. She frequently looks behind her to check if someone is following her and insists on having her back against a wall where she can see everything around her. These behaviors have become increasingly pronounced, especially in environments like her workplace where she feels particularly vulnerable. The memories are not just intrusive; they are also fragmented. While Maria knows what happened, finding the words to describe it is challenging. The olfactory recall intensifies these experiences, making them feel more immediate and real. This vivid recollection leads her to ruminate even more about how she could have prevented or understood the event better. Maria's husband has noticed changes in her behavior over time. She avoids going out alone and becomes visibly distressed when they visit locations that remind her of the war zone. Her work as an auditor, once a source of pride and stability, now feels like a trap. The structured environment seems to heighten her sense of unease rather than provide comfort. What finally brought Maria to seek help was the realization that she could not continue living in this constant state of heightened alertness and fear. She is most afraid of never being able to reclaim her life or her emotions, but at the same time, she hopes for a way to break free from the relentless cycle of memories and maladaptive behaviors. Maria's current state is one of pervasive anxiety and avoidance, with the trauma shaping nearly every aspect of her daily life. The fear that others can see what happened to her has driven her to adopt strategies that only deepen her sense of isolation and helplessness. Her hope lies in finding a way to regain control over her thoughts and emotions, to break free from the overwhelming memories and threats that have come to define her days.
